title: KOSPI Close November 4, 2026: Rises 0.62% to 5,683.80, KOSDAQ +1.50%
content:
KOSPI closed at 5,683.80, up 0.62%, and KOSDAQ closed at 714.95, up 1.50%, after a volatile session in which KOSPI opened up 2.43% and fell as far as 3.27% as U.S. midterm vote counting pointed toward a Democratic majority in Congress. Renewable energy, wind, energy storage (ESS), fuel cell and agricultural robot stocks moved on their own news.

1. Volatile session — U.S. midterms and AI data center worries

KOSPI opened at 5,786.13 (+2.43%) after the Nasdaq (+0.83%) and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (+2.63%) rose the previous day, and climbed to around 5,828 during the session. It turned lower as U.S. midterm vote counting made a Democratic takeover of Congress more likely. At 1:21 p.m. it was down to 5,463.94 (-3.27%), with foreign investors net selling about 2.3319 trillion won. The loss then narrowed, and KOSDAQ briefly fell below 700 to 689.12 (-2.17%). By the close, KOSPI was at 5,683.80 (+0.62%) and KOSDAQ at 714.95 (+1.50%).

2. Solar and renewable energy — hopes for a policy shift

Daemyung Energy, Geumyang Green Power, Hanwha Solutions, HD Hyundai Energy Solutions, OCI Holdings, Dasco and SK Eternix drew attention. Expectations rose that if Democrats take Congress, support for clean energy that the Trump administration has trimmed could change. Democrats have promoted restoring clean energy tax credits and expanding renewable investment. However, a presidential veto remains possible, so the tax credits would not be restored right away; the hope is closer to checking further cuts.

3. Wind power — hopes for easier U.S. permitting

CS Wind, CS Bearing and Taewoong were bought together on hopes that regulation and permitting burdens on wind power in the U.S. could ease. A friendlier policy could restart stalled wind projects and lift new orders, which was the common reason for the rise.

4. ESS and secondary batteries — more renewables, more storage

ESS-related names such as Samsung SDI, Shinheung SEC, GFI, Hanjung NCS, Sangsin EDP and Shinsung ST, and battery materials makers such as L&F, EcoPro BM, POSCO Future M and Enchem drew interest. Solar and wind output fluctuates with the weather, so storage is needed. AI data center power demand and a growing North American ESS market added to the interest, spreading it to battery cells, parts and materials makers. The key point is that a battery industry that relied on electric vehicles is widening its demand to ESS. Many materials stocks rose on sector-wide expectations rather than direct ESS benefits.

5. Fuel cells and distributed power — who pays for data center electricity

Doosan Fuel Cell, Amosense, Vina Tech, Cosesys, Seojin System and Hansun Engineering, names linked to fuel cells and Bloom Energy, drew attention. Both U.S. Democrats and Republicans have pointed out that AI data centers are raising household electricity bills, and discussion grew that data center operators should pay for grid expansion. Hopes that distributed power, where data centers build their own generation, could grow lifted SOFC and power generation fuel cell companies together. Doosan Fuel Cell was grouped in on its own fuel cell business, not as a Bloom Energy supplier.

6. Agricultural robots — Daedong's Saemangeum robot farm factory plan

Daedong Group related stocks, including Daedong, Daedong Gear and Daedong Metal, were strong. Daedong announced a plan with North Jeolla Province, Gimje City and Hyundai Motor Group to build a "physical AI robot farm factory" on about 21 hectares at Saemangeum in 2028–2032, a hub for robot building, AI training and field testing in one place. The 300 billion won figure is the size of the overall concept, not a confirmed investment or order, and the company is still discussing commercialization with the agencies involved.

Quick FAQ

How did KOSPI and KOSDAQ close on Nov 4?
KOSPI closed at 5,683.80 (+0.62%) and KOSDAQ at 714.95 (+1.50%). KOSPI opened at 5,786.13 (+2.43%), fell as far as 5,463.94 (-3.27%) at 1:21 p.m., and then narrowed its loss.

Why did the market swing during the session?
U.S. midterm vote counting pointed toward a Democratic majority in Congress, which raised uncertainty, and foreign investors net sold about 2.3319 trillion won at one point.

Would a Democratic Congress restore clean energy tax credits right away?
No. A presidential veto remains possible, so the hope is closer to checking further cuts than to an immediate restoration.
